body:
Odisha as a regional development of Nagara

Odisha developed a recognisable regional temple tradition commonly called the Kalinga school. It belongs broadly to the Nagara order, but it uses its own terminology and characteristic proportions. Important centres include Bhubaneswar, Puri and Konark.

The main shrine tower is commonly called the deul. It rises above the garbhagriha and often appears almost vertical through much of its height before curving more sharply near the summit. The pillared assembly hall in front of the sanctum is known as the jagamohana.

Unlike the principal deul, the jagamohana often has a stepped pyramidal roof. A learner should therefore examine the whole structure before deciding that a stepped roof makes the temple Dravida.

The three characteristic Odisha roof forms

FormRoof or tower characterTypical association
Rekha deulTall curving tower, rising prominently above the sanctumMain shrine in many Odisha temples
Pidha deulStepped pyramidal roof made from successive horizontal tiersFrequently associated with the jagamohana
Khakhara deulElongated, vaulted or barrel-shaped roofA distinctive Odisha form, often associated with goddess shrines

The rekha deul and pidha deul commonly appear together within the same temple. The former marks the sacred chamber, while the latter covers a connected assembly hall. The khakhara form is an alternative roof type, not simply another name for the stepped jagamohana.

Konark: a Sun temple conceived as a stone chariot

The Sun Temple at Konark, Odisha, is a major achievement of the Kalinga school. It was constructed in the 13th century CE under the patronage of Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty.

The monument is dedicated to Surya, the Sun. Its architectural conception represents a monumental stone chariot. The platform incorporates 24 carved wheels arranged in 12 pairs, decorated with elaborate motifs. In the symbolic conception of the monument, the chariot is drawn by 7 horses; UNESCO records that 6 of their sculpted representations survive.

The chariot idea does not mean that the temple could actually move. The wheels and horses form a fixed sculptural representation integrated into the stone building.

Konark originally had a much taller principal sanctum tower, but that tower no longer survives. Its imposing jagamohana, or assembly hall, remains a principal visible architectural component. The present appearance should therefore not be mistaken for the complete original elevation.

Distinguishing Konark from other Sun temples

Konark and Modhera in Gujarat are both associated with the worship of Surya, but their architectural identities are different. Konark belongs to the Kalinga tradition of Odisha and is famous for its stone chariot and 24 wheels. Modhera belongs to the Maru-Gurjara tradition of western India and is especially associated with a monumental stepped Surya Kund.

Dedication to the same deity does not imply membership in the same regional architectural school. The form of the tower, hall, platform and site arrangement remains essential for identification.

Prelims focus

  • Odisha's Kalinga school is a regional development within the Nagara order.
  • Rekha deul: curving sanctum tower; pidha deul: stepped pyramidal hall roof.
  • Jagamohana: assembly hall in Odisha temple terminology.
  • Konark Sun Temple: Odisha, 13th century CE, Eastern Ganga ruler Narasimhadeva I.
  • Konark's chariot representation includes 24 wheels in 12 pairs.
  • Trap: A stepped jagamohana roof does not make Konark a Dravida temple.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, printed pp. 78–80; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Sun Temple, Konark, Outstanding Universal Value, Brief Synthesis (consulted 23 November 2026); UNESCO World Heritage Centre, ICOMOS evaluation of the Sun Temple at Konark, description of the chariot and surviving horses (consulted 23 November 2026).]

pictures.caption: The Kalinga vocabulary distinguishes the main curving deul from the stepped hall roof.

title: The Kalinga School of Odisha and the Sun Temple at Konark

body:
The principal features of the southern order

Dravida is the principal South Indian order of temple architecture. Its best-known sanctuary tower is the vimana, which commonly rises in a stepped pyramidal form. In contrast to the usual Nagara curvilinear tower, the elevation of a developed Dravida vimana is composed of clearly organised horizontal levels that become smaller towards the top.

Many developed Dravida temple complexes have enclosure walls and monumental entrance towers called gopurams. The principal shrine lies within the enclosure, while the gopuram marks an entrance through the surrounding wall. A temple tank and smaller shrines may also form part of the complex.

Vimana, gopuram and shikhara are not interchangeable

The terms refer to different architectural components:

  • Vimana: The shrine structure and its superstructure, commonly identified by its stepped pyramidal tower in Dravida temples.
  • Gopuram: A monumental entrance tower built over a gateway in the enclosure wall.
  • Shikhara in specialised Dravida usage: The crowning element near the summit of the vimana, rather than the entire tower as the term is commonly used in Nagara descriptions.

This distinction prevents a common error: the tallest entrance gateway of a temple complex is not necessarily the tower over its principal deity.

Temple enclosures and later expansion

As major South Indian temples expanded, additional walls, courtyards, mandapas and gateways could be constructed around older shrines. Consequently, the tallest gopuram in a large temple complex may belong to a later stage of development, while the older sanctum tower is comparatively modest.

The Srirangam temple at Tiruchirappalli is a notable example of expansion through successive enclosures. Its plan contains 7 concentric rectangular enclosure walls with gateways.

Developed South Indian temple architecture also commonly features large dvarapalas, or guardian figures, near sacred entrances. By comparison, Nagara sanctum doorways frequently include figures representing the river goddesses Ganga and Yamuna. These are characteristic decorative tendencies rather than rigid exclusions.

The Pallavas: from carved rock to structural temples

The Pallavas were major patrons of temple building in the Tamil region, particularly during the 7th and 8th centuries CE. Their monuments at Mamallapuram, also called Mahabalipuram, show important stages in the development of South Indian temple forms.

Narasimhavarman I, known as Mamalla, is associated with the great development of rock-cut and monolithic monuments at Mamallapuram. The celebrated Five Rathas are monolithic shrines carved from individual masses of rock. Here, the term ratha describes the form and traditional name of these monuments; they are not wheeled vehicles.

The later Shore Temple is a structural temple, generally associated with Narasimhavarman II, also called Rajasimha, in the early 8th century CE. It is an important example of the emerging structural Dravida tradition.

The Shore Temple complex contains 3 shrines: 2 associated with Shiva and 1 with Vishnu. This combination illustrates that even within an identifiable regional architectural order, individual temple layouts and religious arrangements could vary.

Distinguish construction method from architectural style: The Pallava Five Rathas are monolithic, while the Shore Temple is structural. Both belong to the broader history of Pallava temple architecture.

Prelims focus

  • Dravida architecture is associated chiefly with South India and stepped pyramidal vimanas.
  • Vimana: sanctum superstructure; gopuram: entrance tower.
  • Temple tanks and enclosure walls are prominent features of many developed Dravida complexes.
  • Mamallapuram's Five Rathas are associated with Pallava ruler Narasimhavarman I, Mamalla.
  • The structural Shore Temple is associated with Narasimhavarman II, Rajasimha.
  • Trap: A gopuram is not the same structure as the vimana above the garbhagriha.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, printed pp. 81–84; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 12, Buildings, Paintings and Books, printed p. 124; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram, Outstanding Universal Value, Brief Synthesis (consulted 23 November 2026).]

title: Dravida Architecture: Southern Temple Complexes and Pallava Foundations

body:
Rajaraja I and the building of Brihadisvara

The Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu, is one of the most important monuments of Dravida architecture. It was built under Rajaraja Chola I and was consecrated around 1009–1010 CE.

The temple is also known as Rajarajeshvara or Rajarajeswaram. It is dedicated to Shiva. The association with Rajaraja I is particularly significant because the temple's architecture and inscriptions reflect the resources, organisation and religious patronage of the Chola state.

The Chola rulers controlled an extensive kingdom centred in the Kaveri region. Large temples received endowments and employed numerous specialists. They were therefore not only places of worship but also important centres of cultural and economic life.

The dominant vimana

The most recognisable feature of Brihadisvara is its exceptionally tall, stepped pyramidal vimana. It rises above the garbhagriha in a carefully ordered sequence of diminishing levels. The main superstructure has 13 tiers and is crowned by an upper architectural member.

Unlike some later expanded South Indian temple complexes, where a large entrance gopuram may dominate the skyline, the principal vimana is the overwhelmingly prominent vertical element at Brihadisvara.

The temple also has substantial entrance gateways, enclosing walls, pillared spaces and a Nandi pavilion aligned with the Shiva sanctum. The presence of a large Nandi is consistent with the temple's dedication to Shiva.

Sculpture, inscriptions and paintings

The temple's architecture is accompanied by elaborate sculpture and painted decoration. Important Chola-period murals survive in passages associated with the sanctum. They include Shaiva themes and royal associations.

The inscriptions are a major historical source for the temple's patronage and administration. They help identify Rajaraja I's relationship to the building and record aspects of its resources and activities.

The temple's architectural achievement should therefore be understood in 2 connected ways: its Dravida structural design and the Chola political and cultural setting that made such a large project possible.

Three temples that represent developed Chola architecture

Brihadisvara at Thanjavur belongs to the group known as the Great Living Chola Temples. The other 2 members demonstrate how the architectural tradition continued under later Chola rulers.

TempleLocationRoyal association
BrihadisvaraThanjavur, Tamil NaduRajaraja I; consecrated 1009–1010 CE
Brihadisvara or GangaikondacholisvaramGangaikondacholapuram, Tamil NaduRajendra I; completed 1035 CE
AiravatesvaraDarasuram, Tamil NaduRajaraja II; 12th century CE

Rajendra I, the son and successor of Rajaraja I, built the major Shiva temple at Gangaikondacholapuram. Its vimana has a more gently curving upward profile than the more severe stepped elevation at Thanjavur, while remaining within the Dravida tradition.

The Airavatesvara Temple at Darasuram, associated with Rajaraja II, is smaller and notable for highly elaborate ornamentation. These differences show that Dravida architecture continued to develop instead of reproducing a single unchanging model.

Dynasty and monument association: Rajaraja I belongs with Thanjavur; Rajendra I belongs with Gangaikondacholapuram; Rajaraja II belongs with Darasuram.

Prelims focus

  • Brihadisvara, also called Rajarajeshvara, is at Thanjavur in Tamil Nadu.
  • Builder: Rajaraja Chola I; consecration: 1009–1010 CE.
  • Dedication: Shiva; architectural order: Dravida.
  • The principal vimana has 13 tiers.
  • The Great Living Chola Temples are at Thanjavur, Gangaikondacholapuram and Darasuram.
  • Trap: Rajendra I built at Gangaikondacholapuram; the original Brihadisvara at Thanjavur is associated with Rajaraja I.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, printed pp. 84–85; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 2, New Kings and Kingdoms, printed pp. 22–24, and Chapter 5, Rulers and Buildings, printed pp. 62–64; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Great Living Chola Temples, Outstanding Universal Value, Brief Synthesis (consulted 23 November 2026).]

body:
Understanding the term Vesara

Vesara is a term associated with architectural developments in the Deccan, especially forms that bring together features of the Nagara and Dravida traditions. It is often introduced as a third major temple style, alongside Nagara and Dravida.

The classification requires care. Ancient terminology and modern art-historical classifications do not always apply the word Vesara to exactly the same monuments. Some temples in the Deccan are clearly Nagara, others clearly Dravida, and still others show hybrid characteristics. Vesara is therefore most useful for understanding architectural interaction and regional experimentation, not for treating every Deccan temple as one uniform type.

The early Chalukyas and their major centres

The early Chalukyas of Badami were important patrons of temple architecture in Karnataka from the 6th to the 8th centuries CE. Three major centres associated with their architectural development are Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal.

These centres illustrate the use of rock-cut and structural methods, as well as experimentation with different plans and tower forms.

  • Badami: Known for rock-cut cave monuments and the architectural activity of the early Chalukyas.
  • Aihole: An important centre of experiments with temple plans and roof forms.
  • Pattadakal: A major complex where North Indian and South Indian architectural forms appear within the same group of temples.

The distinctive example of Aihole

The Durga Temple at Aihole is especially notable for its apsidal plan. An apsidal building has an elongated plan ending in a rounded or semicircular portion. This recalls the plan of certain earlier Buddhist chaitya halls.

Although the Durga Temple has a curved rear plan, its tower displays northern architectural characteristics. It illustrates why plan and elevation must both be considered: an unusual ground plan does not automatically determine the form of the superstructure.

Another temple at Aihole, Lad Khan, is significant for its hall-like form, which has been compared with older timber-roofed building traditions. Together these monuments illustrate the variety of approaches explored by Chalukya builders.

Pattadakal and the Virupaksha Temple

Pattadakal is particularly important because its temple group includes monuments using both northern and southern forms. It is therefore a strong example of the exchange of architectural ideas in the Deccan.

The Virupaksha Temple at Pattadakal was commissioned around 740 CE by Queen Lokamahadevi to commemorate the military success of her husband, Vikramaditya II. Its design is an important early example of the Dravida tradition.

This distinction matters: Pattadakal as a site exhibits northern and southern architectural interactions, but that does not mean every temple within the complex must have a completely hybrid tower.

The important exception of the Kailasa Temple at Ellora

The Kailasa or Kailasanatha Temple at Ellora, Maharashtra, is another major Deccan monument. It is generally attributed to Rashtrakuta ruler Krishna I in the 8th century CE.

The temple was carved from a single rock mass and is famous for its immense monolithic excavation. Architecturally, however, it follows a substantially Dravida design, with a vimana and related features.

Do not classify a temple solely by its geographical location. Ellora's Kailasa Temple is in the Deccan and is monolithic, yet its architectural form is Dravida. Similarly, Pattadakal contains individual temples with recognisable Nagara or Dravida features.

Prelims focus

  • Vesara is associated with hybrid architectural developments in the Deccan.
  • Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal are major early Chalukya architectural centres in Karnataka.
  • Durga Temple at Aihole: apsidal plan.
  • Pattadakal's Virupaksha Temple: commissioned by Queen Lokamahadevi around 740 CE.
  • Ellora's Kailasa Temple: Rashtrakuta association, Krishna I, monolithic construction and Dravida architectural form.
  • Trap: A Deccan location or monolithic construction does not automatically make a temple Vesara.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, printed pp. 85–88; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Group of Monuments at Pattadakal, property description (consulted 23 November 2026); Archaeological Survey of India, Ellora Caves, section on Kailasa, Cave 16 (consulted 23 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: Durga, Virupaksha and Kailasa temples show why Deccan location, architectural form and construction method must be considered separately.
pictures.caption: Deccan examples demonstrate architectural interaction without forming one uniform design.

title: Vesara Architecture and the Chalukya Experiments of the Deccan
